title: COBUILD & CEFR 14 Functional Dialogue Archetypes & Register-Isolated Pragmatic Trajectories
description: Unified neuro-symbolic configuration that classifies, merges, register-isolates, and distills all 40 units from speaking_skills_a2.json (U01-U20) and speaking_skills_b1plus.json (U01-U20) plus 6 high-frequency CEFR/EAP spoken interaction domains into 14 Macro Functional Dialogue Archetypes (28 register-isolated 8-turn trajectories across A1_A2 and B1_C2) and 6 reusable Micro-Move Conversational Plugins.

design_principles.zero_forced_passage_vocabulary: Reading passage vocabulary is never forced into dialogue turns. Spoken turns are driven exclusively by communicative functions, register-coherent chunks, and natural scenario flow.
design_principles.scenario_bound_optional_lexis: COBUILD lexical items (e.g. 'give someone a ring', 'pick up', 'postpone') are bound to their specific everyday_scenarios and register with optional=True, never forced across incompatible settings.
design_principles.strict_register_and_role_branch_isolatio: Mutually exclusive conversational sub-strategies (such as speaking to strangers/teachers vs close friends/family, or reacting to good news vs bad news) are strictly isolated into separate trajectories.
design_principles.complete_8_turn_pragmatic_closure: Micro-move units (Type C: describing, circumlocution, interrupting, topic-linking, clarifying, emphatic clefts) plug into Turns 3-6, while Turns 7-8 always execute a complete functional resolution and natural spoken pre-closing/farewell.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague gives instructions about a delivery spreadsheet and you simply don't understand (where a neutral clarification is expected)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: What do you mean? / Sorry, I don't get you. Could you explain again?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: What are you saying?! (challenging / upset intonation — sounds like the colleague is blaming or offending you)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'What do you mean?' is a neutral request for clarification; 'What are you saying?' is a challenging / offended reaction. Using the latter when you are just confused signals that you think the speaker is being unkind or blaming you, rather than that you simply didn't understand.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: An IT colleague is explaining how to use new software and you are lost
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry, you've lost me — could you just go over that last bit again?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: What? You make no sense!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Polite apology + 'just' + request keeps the helper's face intact; a short, sharp command with heavy stress on 'no sense' humiliates the explainer and poisons the interaction.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A receptionist gives complex registration instructions over the phone
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Let me just check that I've got it right — I book the slot online, then bring the original documents, then pay in person. Is that right?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: [nods silently, says 'Okay, fine, okay'] — later follows the instructions in the wrong order and makes a costly error
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Silent nodding masks confusion and guarantees a later breakdown; actively paraphrasing back ('So, if I understand you correctly...') is a professional norm in phone/service exchanges.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague states an incorrect deadline in a team meeting ('We're submitting the proposal next Friday')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry to interrupt, but could I just point out that the deadline is actually this Friday?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Wait! You're wrong! It's this Friday, not next Friday!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The softened form combines apology + modal + 'just', which lowers the imposition and protects the other person's face; the blunt form attacks the speaker rather than correcting the fact.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Someone keeps interrupting while you are making an important point
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm sorry — I haven't finished yet, could you just let me finish that thought?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Stop talking and listen to me!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Firm but neutral tone on 'I haven't finished' reclaims the floor without aggression; a command form with heavy stress escalates conflict and alienates the listeners.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend is mid-story about their new job when you remember you need your passport back
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry, I'm getting so carried away! Oh, and by the way — do you have my passport? I'd better pack it for Monday.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I need my passport back — I'm off on vacation on Monday, so I need it today.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Without a transition marker the switch is jarring and the story is dropped mid-air; 'Oh, and by the way' / 'Sorry, before I forget' softens the pivot and signals the return.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A work meeting is going well; you want to raise a serious personal question
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: This may be off-topic, but could I ask about your availability for the new team next month?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: By the way, are you seeing anyone at all? Anyway — what does your partner do for a living?
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'By the way' frames a minor aside; using it to launch a heavy or personal subject in a professional context feels casual and intrusive.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Talking about the amount of belongings to move to a new flat
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I've got loads of stuff to box up—so many things!
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I've got many staff. / I've got a stuff to move. (wrong uncountable form — *many stuff* / *a staff*)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Stuff' is uncountable, so it takes 'much/loads of/lots of some', never *many* or *a / a stuff*; 'things' is countable and takes 'a / this / many / these'.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Borrowing study notes from a classmate
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Can I borrow your notes for tonight?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Can you borrow me your notes? (mixed-up direction between 'borrow' and 'lend')
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: You are borrowing from the other person ('I borrow your notes'); they are lending to you ('You lend me your notes'). Mixing up the two reverses the direction of ownership.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: In a hardware / department store, a customer cannot recall the English word for a corkscrew
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: It's a thing you use for twisting the top off a wine bottle — it's like a little spiral wire, with a handle...?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: [long silence, then switches to the first language: 'cór... corchero...'] or says nothing and browses shelves wordlessly
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Freezing or dropping into L1 breaks the service interaction; circumlocution ('a thing you use for + -ing') with a rising, questioning pitch invites the assistant to supply the word.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Listener helping a speaker who is struggling with a word
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh, I know what you mean — a colander! Yes? A big metal one with holes?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, that's not a screw — a corkscrew is completely different. Look at the label.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Warm, enthusiastic confirmation ('Oh, I know what you mean!') keeps the speaker's confidence up; blunt negation of the speaker's attempt makes them feel embarrassed and shut down.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Describing a gift you genuinely dislike
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I really don't like it, to be honest — I can't even use it. Oh, but thank you all the same.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I don't really like it... I mean, you didn't have to spend money on it. (mild framing when the listener reads it as a total rejection)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'I really don't like it' (emphasis on the negative) = strong dislike; 'I don't really like it' = hedged mild dislike. The position swap is the meaning shift and a frequent source of misinterpretation between speakers.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague claims, 'You never send the reports on time'
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I DID send the report on Friday, I'm sure — it's in your inbox, just check.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I sent it on Friday, I think... maybe. (flat, unemphasized)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Placing nuclear stress on the auxiliary ('I did phone you! / I did send it!') is the English marker of contradiction of a false assumption; a flat, unstressed re-assertion reads as a weak denial and leaves the accusation standing.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Agreeing with a negative statement ('I didn't really enjoy the trip' / 'I'm not keen on spicy food' / 'I don't really like studying here')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: No, me neither. / Me neither. I don't like spicy food at all.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Me too. / Me too. I don't like it at all. (wrong polarity — positive agreement to a negative statement)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Me too' is used only for positive statements ('I liked... / I enjoy...'); 'me neither' is used for negative statements ('I didn't... / I'm not...'). Mixing them up signals a fundamental grammar misalignment in the agreement.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Upgrading a comment to show enthusiasm ('good -> really good', 'nice -> really nice / delicious')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: It was really good. And knowledgeable too. (emphatic stress on REALLY / KNOWLEDGEABLE)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: It was good. And knowledgeable too. (no emphatic stress on the upgraded adjective — sounds flat, like an unenthusiastic repeat)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The upgraded adjective (REALLY, TERRIBLE, AMAZING, DELICIOUS) needs prominent emphatic stress and a wider pitch range to signal genuine enthusiasm; without it the upgrade reads as an unenthusiastic repeat of the original comment.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Genuine enquiry: uncertain whether the listener agrees with your assessment of a new restaurant
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: It's a lovely café, don't you think? (rising intonation — a genuine question)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: It's a lovely café, don't you think? (flat falling intonation — expects agreement / demands consent)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Falling tags ask for confirmation ('you agree?'); rising tags ask a genuine question when you are unsure. Using the falling form when seeking a real opinion sounds leading or pushy.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: After the speaker finishes telling a long story about their holiday (risk of conversation hijacking)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: That sounds amazing — you must have had a great time. Anyway, you were saying...?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Oh, I know about that — my sister went to Japan last year and her flight was delayed for two days...
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Stealing the floor with your own story right after their story feels like the conversation was about you; use a brief acknowledgment plus 'you were saying...?' to hand the floor back.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Proposing a dinner arrangement to a friend on the phone
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Fancy coming round for dinner tonight?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Fancy to come round for dinner tonight? (infinitive after 'fancy')
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Fancy' takes a gerund (-ing) or a noun ('Fancy coming...?', 'Fancy the idea...?'), never a 'to + base verb' infinitive—'Fancy to come...' is a clear A2-level grammar error.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Postponing a lunch date because you are running late (tone)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm so sorry, I'm running late. Can we make it tomorrow? (genuine, soft, apologetic tone)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I'm running late. Can we make it tomorrow? (flat, curt, irritated tone — no apology, no pitch movement)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Postponing an arrangement needs soft, down-tone apology with a rising question at the end to sound genuine; a flat, curt delivery sounds impatient and dismissive.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking to be connected to a named person on the phone
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Good evening, can I speak to Mr Dawson, please?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Good evening, can I call to Mr Dawson, please? / Sorry I can't leave your call. / Can you listen me now? (wrong collocations)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Phone collocations are fixed ('speak to', 'take your call', 'get back to', 'hear me', 'leave a message'); mixing them up ('call to', 'listen me', 'leave your call') signals a non-native speaker immediately on the phone.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Refusing a persistent telemarketer who won't take 'no' for an answer (escalating firmness)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: [Mmm...] thank you, but I, [um], don't want to change contract. -> [Er], no, I'm really not interested. -> [Sigh] Listen, I'm not interested. Now, thank you for calling, but my answer is no. Goodbye.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No. No. No. (immediate, flat, curt — no hesitation sounds, no gradual escalation)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Hesitation sounds ('er', 'um', 'mmm') and a sigh build the refusal; escalation from polite but firm ('thank you, but...') to firm and final ('Listen, I'm not interested') signals growing disinterest while keeping you socially acceptable.

communication_tips: Use the prepositions and chunks accurately: 'meet at 10 a.m., on Friday, free for lunch / tennis, going for a walk / coffee, pick you up, look forward to seeing you'.

Use informal language ('Fancy coming round...?', 'Let's say 7 p.m.?') with friends, and formal language ('Would you be able to attend...?', 'Shall we say Friday at 10 a.m.?') in professional situations.
Sound enthusiastic when accepting ('Great, see you later!') and genuinely apologetic when postponing ('I'm running late. Can we make it tomorrow?').

Your responses control how a conversation develops: short, flat one-word responses ('Mmm.', 'Right.') when you want to end it, and short questions or excited exclamations ('Really?', 'No way!', 'Wow!') when you want to develop it.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: You meet an old friend on the street but are late for an appointment
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Anyway, look, I really must go — but it's been great seeing you. Let's catch up soon for a proper cup of tea!
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Bye. (turns and walks off in the middle of the chat)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A bare 'Bye' with no reason, no pleasure, and no future contact is a flat, abrupt cut-off; the three-step close (reason + pleasure + future contact) signals a warm, socially complete ending.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Your partner is signalling they need to leave ('Mmm, well, I've got a lot to do...')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh, of course — well, it's been lovely catching up. Let's keep in touch, yeah?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Really? Well, I've still got a hundred things to tell you about the holiday...
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Missing the pre-closing cues (fillers + mention of obligation) forces your partner to interrupt you; releasing them promptly is the expected norm.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Declining a colleague's invitation to a karaoke night
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Thanks for asking, that's sweet of you! Karaoke isn't really my kind of thing, I'm afraid. How about I bring the snacks next time, though?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, I don't want to go. (cold, no thanks, no reason)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A bare 'No' to an invitation reads as rejection of the person, not just the event; the expected bundle is thanks + soft preference + a plausible or future-goodwill note, keeping the relationship intact.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Refusing a manager's request for weekend overtime
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'd really like to help out, but I'm afraid it's not a good time — I've got something else on that weekend. If it's really urgent, I could come in a couple of hours though.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No. (and walks away — no thanks, no apology, no reason)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: In a hierarchical request the refusal must still open with appreciation / softener and offer a narrow concession; a flat, ungracious 'No' reads as insubordinate and damages the relationship.

communication_tips: Watch for signals that the other person needs to leave.
Signal the pre-closing clearly ('Anyway...').
State that you enjoyed the conversation.
Give a brief, plausible reason why you have to go.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Saying the price of a 2.50 pound item
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: That comes to two pounds fifty, please.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: That's two and a half pounds. (wrong money phrase for £2.50)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: For whole pounds you can say 'X pounds', but for £2.50 the correct British form is 'two pounds fifty' (or 'two fifty'); 'two and a half pounds' is wrong for this amount.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Buying time before a price decision (pause after a thinking phrase)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Let me see, [pause] OK, that sounds good.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Let me see OK that sounds good. (no pause — sounds rushed, like a statement)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Let me see / think' is a deliberate buying-time device; a micro-pause signals you are thinking, then a natural decision follows. Rushing both phrases together sounds automatic and uncooperative.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Talking about the amount of belongings to move to a new flat
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I've got loads of stuff to box up—so many things!
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I've got many staff. / I've got a stuff to move. (wrong uncountable form — *many stuff* / *a staff*)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Stuff' is uncountable, so it takes 'much/loads of/lots of some', never *many* or *a / a stuff*; 'things' is countable and takes 'a / this / many / these'.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Borrowing study notes from a classmate
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Can I borrow your notes for tonight?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Can you borrow me your notes? (mixed-up direction between 'borrow' and 'lend')
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: You are borrowing from the other person ('I borrow your notes'); they are lending to you ('You lend me your notes'). Mixing up the two reverses the direction of ownership.

communication_tips: Be precise with money: '£2,500.00' is 'two and a half thousand pounds' (✓), whereas '£2.50' is 'two pounds fifty' (never *two and a half pounds*); you can say '50p' (pee) or '50 pence'.
In informal British English, people often say 'quid' for 'pounds' ('twenty quid').

Pause briefly after thinking phrases ('Let me see, [pause] OK, that sounds good', 'Let me think, [pause] I'll take those, please') and link initial auxiliary chunks ('Do_you_have_any...', 'Can_I get...', 'Could_I book...').

Spoken landmark questions while giving directions ('See the cafe on the corner?' / 'You know the Empire State building?') drop auxiliary verbs, so they are shorter than their written equivalents ('Can you see...?' / 'Do you know...?').

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Talking about office rumour that a new manager is arriving
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I've only just heard it, but apparently they're bringing in a new manager next week — or so I'm told.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: They're definitely bringing in a new manager next week. I know it's true.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Presenting second-hand information as an absolute fact is risky socially and professionally; hedged reporting ('apparently', 'so I'm told') sounds more credible and protects your face if the rumour is false.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague asks about salary at the office
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm sure the pay isn't bad, as far as I know. What about you — what sort of thing do you get?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: How much did they pay you? Come on, tell me!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A rapid, direct wh-question about a sensitive topic feels like an interrogation; the indirect version gives the other person an easy way out and shares your own (honest) information first.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: In a hardware / department store, a customer cannot recall the English word for a corkscrew
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: It's a thing you use for twisting the top off a wine bottle — it's like a little spiral wire, with a handle...?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: [long silence, then switches to the first language: 'cór... corchero...'] or says nothing and browses shelves wordlessly
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Freezing or dropping into L1 breaks the service interaction; circumlocution ('a thing you use for + -ing') with a rising, questioning pitch invites the assistant to supply the word.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Listener helping a speaker who is struggling with a word
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh, I know what you mean — a colander! Yes? A big metal one with holes?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, that's not a screw — a corkscrew is completely different. Look at the label.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Warm, enthusiastic confirmation ('Oh, I know what you mean!') keeps the speaker's confidence up; blunt negation of the speaker's attempt makes them feel embarrassed and shut down.

communication_tips: Offer your own information first to build trust before asking.
Ask indirect or tag questions rather than interrogating.
Use the person's name and inclusive pronouns ('we', 'us', 'our').
Clearly distinguish verified facts from hearsay and rumour.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking a stranger to move their coat from a reserved seat on the train
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Excuse me, would you mind moving your coat, please?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Would you mind help me move your coat? / Do you mind if I paying...? / Is it OK if I'm using your bag? (wrong verb form after the request frame)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Would you mind' + -ing, 'Could you' + base verb, and 'Do you mind if I' / 'Is it OK if I' + present simple are fixed frames; switching the verb form (help / paying / calling) is an obvious A2-level grammar error.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking a stranger for directions or a photo
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry, could you possibly take our photo, please? ↗ (polite rising intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Could you possibly take our photo, please? ↘ (flat, falling intonation — reads as an order, not a request)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Requests to strangers should close with a small rising intonation cue (a soft 'please' or an open question tone) rather than a strong falling, full-stop intonation that sounds like an order.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Thanking grandparents for an expensive graduation gift
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Thank you so much for the present. I really appreciate it. (warm, sincere intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Cheers! (flat, casual intonation — reads as dismissive for a big, thoughtful gift)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Cheers' is a short, light British informal token for small casual favours (passing a pen); using it for an expensive gift from grandparents reads as dismissive and casual when a warmer 'Thank you so much for the present' is expected at this register.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Declining a Saturday picnic invitation
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'd love to, but I'm visiting my sister this weekend. Thanks for asking! (soft, regretful intonation, warm 'thanks')
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, I'm busy. (blunt refusal, no reason, no thanks — flat, curt, sounds rude)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A polite British-style declination always softens the refusal with 'I'd love to, but...', gives a reason, and finishes with a warm 'Thanks for asking'; a flat 'No, I'm busy' without any of these is perceived as rude and dismissive.

communication_tips: Use indirect questions with rising intonation in formal situations or with strangers ('Excuse me, would you mind taking our photo, please?', 'Sorry, could you possibly explain that again, please?').
Use direct questions in informal situations with friends and family ('Can I use your mobile, Mark?').
When declining an invitation or offer, it is polite to say 'I'd love to, but...', explain why you are busy, and then thank the person ('Thanks for asking').
Use the full verb structure 'I'd like to thank [my family] for + -ing [supporting me]' in formal situations and speeches (weddings, graduations, or awards).

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague asks, 'Would you mind closing the window?'
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Not at all — of course not, I'll do it now.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Yes, of course! (meaning: yes, I am happy to do it)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Would you mind...?' is polarity-reversed: a literal 'yes' agrees with the word 'mind' (= refusal). The idiomatic granting is 'Not at all' / 'No, of course not' — a classic trap for learners and L1 speakers.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking a host about using a chair in their home
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Would you mind if I took the blue chair? Is it all right?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Would you mind if I take the blue chair right now?
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: After 'Would you mind if I ...' English requires the past (hypothetical) form — 'opened / took' — to mark the tentative, polite frame; the present tense breaks the formula and sounds abrupt.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking a busy colleague to proofread a document for you
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm really sorry to bother you, but would it be at all possible for you to proofread my report before Friday?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Check my report now. It's urgent.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A bare imperative for a big favour is a register clash between the size of the imposition and the directness of the form; an apologetic opener + high-indirectness formula matches the social context.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend compliments your new jacket ('What a great-looking jacket — it really suits you!')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Thank you! I'm really glad you like it — I actually got it in the sales.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, it's cheap and ugly, don't bother. It washes out terribly.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A flat denial forces the giver to awkwardly contradict you or retreat; a warm 'Thank you' + brief detail (or a small question like 'Do you think so?') accepts the compliment while sounding sincere.

communication_tips: Match the indirectness of the request to the size of the favour and your relationship with the person.
Start with an apology for big favours ('I'm sorry to bother you, but...').
Give the other person an easy way out ('Is there any chance...?').
If you have to refuse, apologize and explain briefly.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Reassuring a friend or student who is panicking or stressed
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh dear, I'm really sorry. OK, OK, calm down — let's figure this out together. (low, gentle, slightly slower intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Oh dear! Calm down! Don't worry! (fast, high-pitch, impatient delivery — sounds dismissive or annoyed)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Sympathy is prosodic: a low, gentle tone with a slightly slower pace signals empathy; a fast, high-pitch delivery of 'Oh dear!' and 'Calm down!' reads as impatient and dismissive of the person's feelings.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Comforting a friend who has just failed her driving test or had a car accident
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh, I'm so sorry. Oh dear! I know how you feel. — (slow pace, low tone, gentle intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Cheer up! It's not the end of the world! (fast, high, dismissive, full-stop intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Sympathy is delivered in a lower, slower, gentler tone; a fast, high-pitched 'Cheer up!' sounds dismissive and insensitive — it signals to the listener that their pain is over-stated rather than being shared.

communication_tips: Use 'If I were you, I'd...' to give advice and make suggestions (similar meaning to 'You could...'): 'If I were you, I'd look for another job'.
When listening to someone with a problem, speak gently and in a low, sympathetic tone ('Oh dear. That's not fair').
Use these expressions to make someone feel better: 'Never mind.', 'Don't worry about it.', 'Try not to worry.'
Learn the three distinct patterns for talking about pain: 'I've got a pain in my leg' (noun), 'My leg's very painful' (adjective), 'I'm in pain' (prepositional phrase).

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Asking a friend for help choosing between two job offers
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Can you give me some advice? What do you think I should do?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Can you give me an advice? Or maybe some advices?
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Advice' is uncountable; 'an advice' or 'advices' is a visible grammar trap. The natural spoken quantifier is 'some' or 'a piece of / a bit of'.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend is torn between a high-paying job and a closer-commute job
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh no, that's a really tough call. If it was me, I'd weigh up the salary against the commute — have you thought about asking both for remote days?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: You have to quit your job! What are you thinking? It's obvious what you should do.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Imperative commands with zero empathy are read as a lecture or an intrusion into the friend's autonomy; a tentative, empathetic frame ('If I were you...') keeps the advice collaborative.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend is nervous before a job interview
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Nervous? That's only natural — you're overqualified for it. Just give it your best shot: what's the worst that could happen?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Stop being silly, it's easy. Any idiot can do that interview.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Minimizing the anxiety ('Stop being silly') invalidates the feeling; the expected English move acknowledges the feeling, lowers the stakes, and then encourages ('give it your best shot').

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague learning new software is struggling with the first task
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I know, it's a bit of a beast at first — but you're on the right track, keep going! It'll click soon.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: You're not getting it? Honestly, most people learn this in a day. (flat, sceptical)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Praising specific progress ('You're coming along really well') keeps the learner going; a sceptical comparison to 'most people' reads as put-down and shuts learning down.

communication_tips: Show empathy for the person's situation before jumping in with advice.
Frame advice tentatively ('Have you thought about...?', 'If I were you...') rather than giving orders ('You must...').
Warn gently about consequences where relevant ('Whatever you do, don't...').
Acknowledge the other person's anxiety without dismissing it.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Discussing the actor in a film you both just watched
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Well, to be honest, I'm not a big fan of his. Actually, I really enjoyed it, though. (soft intonation, 'well' as a buffer, then positive contrast)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: He's a terrible actor! (blunt attack, full-stop intonation, no buffer, no softening)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A buffered 'Well, to be honest, ...' + 'not a big fan of' + non-angry intonation reads as a polite personal opinion; a full-stop 'He's a terrible actor!' reads as an attack on the other person's taste and invites conflict.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: An unexpected offensive or confusing remark is made — the listener signals shock / disagreement
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: EXCUSE me? ↗ (strong rising, challenging intonation — signals shock / disagreement: 'What did you just say?!')
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Excuse me. (flat, neutral intonation — just gets someone's attention, no challenge)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The same phrase 'Excuse me' with a strong, high, rising, challenging intonation signals shock or disagreement (as in 'What did you just say?!'); the identical words with flat, falling or neutral intonation just get someone's attention or ask them to repeat.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Ending a heated disagreement that is starting to escalate (de-escalating)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Well, I suppose I can see your point. I guess you have your opinion and I have mine — we'll just have to agree to differ. (soft, slightly smiling intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: That's ridiculous! / Are you serious? (re-starting the challenge, high-pitch, confrontational intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A good closer softens the challenge ('Well, I suppose I can see your point') and offers an 'agree to differ' line; a second wave of 'Are you serious?' or 'That's ridiculous!' re-ignites the conflict and signals the conversation is not actually over.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Agreeing with a negative statement ('I didn't really enjoy the trip' / 'I'm not keen on spicy food' / 'I don't really like studying here')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: No, me neither. / Me neither. I don't like spicy food at all.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Me too. / Me too. I don't like it at all. (wrong polarity — positive agreement to a negative statement)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Me too' is used only for positive statements ('I liked... / I enjoy...'); 'me neither' is used for negative statements ('I didn't... / I'm not...'). Mixing them up signals a fundamental grammar misalignment in the agreement.

communication_tips: Use 'Well, ...' (often with 'to be honest') to introduce a negative opinion someone may not like — it sounds much more polite ('Well, to be honest, I'm not a big fan of his').
Choose polite words and phrases so you don't offend people, use natural linking ('I'm just_saying', 'What_I mean_is', 'I know_what_you_mean, but', 'I suppose_so, but'), and use non-angry intonation.
Even in a strong disagreement, it is polite to show you understand the other person's viewpoint first ('Yeah, OK, I get your point. But...', 'Well, I suppose I can see your point').

Use complete phrases for interrupting / holding the floor: 'No, let me stop you there.' (Stop speaking, because I want to speak); 'Can I just say that...' / 'Can I say something?' (I'd like to speak / add a counter-point).

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Making a strong point at a staff meeting about a remote-work pilot
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm completely sure the pilot should continue — I'm totally convinced the data backs it up.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I'm utterly sure the pilot must continue. It's completely convinced we should expand.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Utterly' collocates with 'convinced', not 'sure'; 'completely / absolutely' collocates with 'sure'. Mixed-strength intensifier+adjective combinations are a visible collocation trap and dilute the rhetorical force.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Disagreeing with a manager's budget proposal in a formal meeting
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm sorry, I can't quite agree with you there — I see what you mean, although the numbers suggest the training budget really needs to stay.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Rubbish! No way is that going to work! (pointing, heavy stress)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Rubbish!' and 'No way!' are informal-blasters reserved for close friends; in a hierarchical professional setting they breach face and register. The softened, partially-conceding form is the expected professional register.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend complains about endless afternoons of meetings
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Tell me about it! I've got four back-to-back today too — it's ridiculous.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: [interpreting 'Tell me about it' literally and asking] 'Well, what exactly would you like me to tell you about it?'
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'Tell me about it!' is emphatic, informal agreement ('I know it from experience!'), not an invitation to narrate. Taking it literally breaks solidarity and sounds flat / pedantic.

communication_tips: Invite quieter participants into the discussion.
Distinguish clearly between personal opinions and objective facts.
Calibrate the strength of your opinion (hedged / neutral vs. strong conviction).
Express full agreement warmly and specifically.

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 1 (Turns 1-2: Opening & Purpose)

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (paraphrase the opening purpose, motivation, or situation actually established in Turns 1-2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (use a detail mentioned later in the dialogue as if it were the opening reason)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Speaker / Role Swap (swap the roles, intentions, or situations of Speaker 1 and Speaker 2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Tone / Polarity Flip (misread the speaker's opening attitude or flip affirmative/negative intent)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 2 (Turns 3-4: Key Question, Point or Constraint)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: What counter-argument or practical drawback does Speaker 2 raise?

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (accurately restate the specific question, requirement, or point Speaker 1 raises around Turn 3)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Opposite Detail / Polarity Flip (invert the key detail, timeframe, or condition mentioned in the dialogue)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (borrow a detail from Turns 5-8 that belongs to a different point)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Overstatement / Scope Distortion (exaggerate a reasonable question or requirement into an extreme rule)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 2 (Turns 3-4: Speaker 2's Response, Experience or Stance)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: How does Speaker 1 clarify their position, and what safeguard does Speaker 2 emphasize?

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (capture Speaker 2's actual response, experience, or perspective in Turn 4—whether affirmative, negative, or conditional)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Opposite Stance / Experience Flip (claim the opposite of what Speaker 2 actually said about their experience or view)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Speaker / Role Swap (attribute Speaker 1's words or expectations to Speaker 2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (mix in a detail from another turn out of context)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 3 (Turns 5-6: Practical Arrangement, Condition or Follow-Up)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: What core distinction or priority does Speaker 1 highlight to bridge their views?

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (capture the schedule, method, or conditional arrangement actually discussed across Turns 5-6)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Condition / Availability Flip (invert which day, time, or condition works vs. doesn't work in the dialogue)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Unadopted / Confused Detail Trap (present a busy conflict or rejected option as the agreed plan)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Overstatement Trap (turn a specific or conditional statement into an extreme absolute)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 4 (Turns 7-8: Next Steps & Closing Outcome)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: On what balanced conclusion do both speakers ultimately agree?

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (identify the final agreed action, timeline, or next step established in Turns 7-8)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Timeline / Action Mix-up (alter the time, day, or next step mentioned at the end of the dialogue)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Speaker / Role Swap (reverse which speaker will take the follow-up action)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: False Outcome Trap (claim the issue was left unresolved or cancelled when they actually reached an agreement)

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Suggesting a Saturday plan to a friend
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: How about going to the beach in the morning? Or we could try the new café afterwards.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: How about go to the beach in the morning? I'd rather to stay at home.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'How about / What about / fancy' require an -ing or noun, and 'I'd rather' takes the bare infinitive; the infinitive errors make the speaker sound non-native and distract from the collaborative tone.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Rejecting a colleague's suggestion for a team curry night
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: To be honest, I really don't fancy going out tonight — I tell you what, how about we do a quiet coffee instead?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, that's boring. It's a waste of time.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A flat, unsoftened refusal attacks the idea (and implicitly the proposer); an apology / soften + negative preference + alternative keeps the relationship and the plan alive.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague gives instructions about a delivery spreadsheet and you simply don't understand (where a neutral clarification is expected)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: What do you mean? / Sorry, I don't get you. Could you explain again?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: What are you saying?! (challenging / upset intonation — sounds like the colleague is blaming or offending you)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: 'What do you mean?' is a neutral request for clarification; 'What are you saying?' is a challenging / offended reaction. Using the latter when you are just confused signals that you think the speaker is being unkind or blaming you, rather than that you simply didn't understand.

communication_tips: Use questions rather than imperatives to sound collaborative.
If rejecting someone's suggestion, apologize and explain why before offering an alternative.
State preferences politely rather than flatly refusing.

If you simply don't understand what someone says, ask politely: 'What do you mean?'. If someone says something that upsets or offends you, use the more aggressive / challenging 'What are you saying?'.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Rejecting a colleague's suggestion for a team curry night
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: To be honest, I really don't fancy going out tonight — I tell you what, how about we do a quiet coffee instead?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: No, that's boring. It's a waste of time.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A flat, unsoftened refusal attacks the idea (and implicitly the proposer); an apology / soften + negative preference + alternative keeps the relationship and the plan alive.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague states an incorrect deadline in a team meeting ('We're submitting the proposal next Friday')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry to interrupt, but could I just point out that the deadline is actually this Friday?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Wait! You're wrong! It's this Friday, not next Friday!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The softened form combines apology + modal + 'just', which lowers the imposition and protects the other person's face; the blunt form attacks the speaker rather than correcting the fact.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Someone keeps interrupting while you are making an important point
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm sorry — I haven't finished yet, could you just let me finish that thought?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Stop talking and listen to me!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Firm but neutral tone on 'I haven't finished' reclaims the floor without aggression; a command form with heavy stress escalates conflict and alienates the listeners.

communication_tips: Use questions rather than imperatives to sound collaborative.
If rejecting someone's suggestion, apologize and explain why before offering an alternative.
State preferences politely rather than flatly refusing.
Apologise before interrupting ('Sorry to interrupt, but...').

pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Sorry, but I'm afraid this chicken isn't quite cooked. (polite hedge, low-confident intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: That's not good enough! / I'm really disappointed with your service! (aggressive intonation and escalation on a first complaint)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A first or minor complaint should begin with a polite hedge ('There seems to be a problem... / I'm afraid...' / 'Sorry, but...'); using the strongest, most confrontational phrasing ('That's not good enough!') before the service side has had a chance to apologise reads as rude and confrontational.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: An agent responding to a serious complaint with a sincere apology
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm so sorry we let you down. Can I offer you a full refund? (low, sincere tone, soft but firm intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I'm so sorry we let you down. (fast, high, robotic, flat tone — sounds insincere / script-reading)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A sincere apology requires a low, slower, softer tone with a natural pause after 'I'm so sorry'; a fast, high, robotic delivery of the same words reads as insincere, scripted, or dismissive of the customer's experience.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Apologising for a small social slip in a casual conversation with a close friend
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm so sorry about last night — I was tired and a bit grumpy. Can I make it up to you? (warm, slightly self-mocking tone)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I wanted to apologise for my behaviour last night. I really regret it. (formal, detached intonation — sounds like a lawyer)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: To a close friend, a strong but warm 'I'm so sorry about last night' with a slightly self-mocking, softer intonation is appropriate; the formal 'apologise for' + 'I really regret it' combo is too stiff for casual friends and can sound cold and distancing.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Apologising for getting presentation figures wrong to a boss (professional context)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I'm really sorry for getting the figures wrong. It was my mistake. (confident, low, sincere intonation — a 'real apology')
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I'm sorry I got the figures... wrong. (flat, fast, insincere — sounds like a half-baked script)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Pronounce the contractions clearly ('I'm', 'my') and land on the apology word ('sorry') with genuine, low intonation; a rushed, flat delivery signals the apology is a script, not a real one, and will be treated as insincere by the listener.

communication_tips: Use hedging verbs like 'seem' and 'appear' ('There seems to be a problem with the screen') or softeners like 'I don't want to make a fuss, but...' to make complaints polite.
Use strong specific phrases ('That's not good enough', 'I'm really disappointed with your service') to escalate a serious complaint.
'I'm afraid...' means 'I'm sorry to tell you that...' and can be placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: 'I'm afraid we're very busy today' / 'We do need the receipt, I'm afraid'.
Sound confident and firm when making a complaint, and sincere / honest when apologizing or responding to one.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Comforting a friend who missed a deadline and lost the client project
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: You must be really disappointed — I can see why it's got you down. Let me know if there's anything I can do.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: You must be really disappointing right now. (wrong participle)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: '-ed' marks the FEELING (a person is disappointed); '-ing' marks the CAUSE (a disappointing result). Swapping them inverts the meaning: '*You are disappointing*' is a harsh criticism, not sympathy.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A manager tells an employee their promotion application / project bid wasn't successful
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I've got something to tell you, I'm afraid. I'm really pleased with the quality of the work, but I'm afraid I've got some bad news: the bid wasn't successful this time.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Your design was rejected. That's it. (flat, no softener)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A blunt statement with no cushion, no positive frame, and no support reads as careless and cold; the expected pattern is warning phrase + honest core + positive note or comfort, delivered at a slightly slower, warmer pace.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A customer speaks to a hotel receptionist about a billing error (charged for two nights, stayed one)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Excuse me if I'm out of line, but I think there's been a bit of a misunderstanding — I was only one night, but I've been charged for two. Could you see what you can do about it?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: You ruined my stay and you're incompetent! I want to speak to your manager, now!
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The softened opener + 'misunderstanding' keeps the other person's face intact and opens a fix path; the personal attack escalates defensiveness, triggers the manager, and usually loses the customer the refund.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A flatmate has been using the other's coffee supplies without asking
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Don't get me wrong — it's great coffee — but in future, would you mind just checking with me before using my supplies? I buy quite specific bags.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Stop stealing my stuff! You're always doing this! (heavy stress, pointing)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Framing as a recurring habit ('you keep using my things without asking') + a concrete request is constructive and face-saving; the personal accusation ('stealing', 'always') turns a small domestic dispute into a character attack.

communication_tips: Signal bad news gently with a warning phrase so it isn't a shock.
Sandwich negative feedback with positive acknowledgement where honest.
Show empathy when receiving somebody else's bad news.
Offer practical help or consolation afterwards.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Greeting someone new or catching up with a friend ('Lovely to meet you' / 'What's your news?')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Hiya, and you! It's been ages. How are you doing? (delivered with lively, interested intonation and linked words)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: How are you doing. Nice to meet you. (delivered in a flat, monotone voice without pitch movement)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Sounding interested requires lively pitch range; flat intonation when saying 'Nice to meet you' or 'What's your news?' makes the speaker sound bored and unfriendly.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Using question tags in small talk ('It's very busy, ...' / 'You didn't like your old job, ...')
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: It's very busy, isn't it? / You didn't like your old job, did you?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: It's very busy, is it? / You didn't like your old job, didn't you?
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Positive statements require a negative question tag ('isn't it?'), and negative statements require a positive question tag ('did you?').

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Congratulating a close family member or friend on a major achievement (a job, a degree, a relationship)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh, well done! I'm so proud of you! I'm really, really pleased for you! (wide-pitch, excited, rising on the exclamation mark)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Well done. I'm proud for you. I'm pleased of you. (flat, low, jealous, full-stop intonation + wrong prepositions)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Genuine congratulations require a wide, high-pitched, rising, excited intonation and a small exclamation-mark stress ('WELL done!'); the same words in a flatter, falling, low-pitch intonation read as jealous, cold, or dismissive. Also note the preposition: it's 'pleased FOR you', 'proud OF you', 'kind OF you' — these pairings are fixed.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Receiving good news from a friend and responding with gratitude (correct prepositions)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Thank you, that's really kind of you. I can't believe I'm over the moon! (warm, excited, sincere intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Thanks a lot, that's really kind to you. (wrong preposition 'to' + flat, bored intonation)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: The prepositions that follow 'kind', 'proud', 'pleased', and 'for / of / to' are fixed and non-optional: 'kind of you' (not 'to you'), 'pleased for you' (not 'of you'), 'proud of you' (not 'for you'); using the wrong preposition here is a classic A2-level collocation error.

communication_tips: Notice how friends introduce each other informally without long phrases: 'Karen, Ben. Ben, Karen.'
Remember to sound interested when meeting someone new—your intonation is as important as eye contact and shaking hands.
It is polite to congratulate someone and then ask how they feel ('Are you nervous?', 'How are you feeling?') to show genuine interest in their good news.
Use 'so' before adjectives to emphasize the emotion: 'I'm excited' → 'I'm so excited!', 'I'm so happy!', 'I'm so pleased'.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Answering 'How did you get here?' to a fellow guest or colleague
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: By train, actually — it took ages, but the view was brilliant. Did you come from far away?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: By train.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A monotone, two-word reply with no follow-up reads as cold or defensive; bright tone + a small extra detail + a reciprocal question keeps the conversation alive.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A friend tells you a travel disaster (lost luggage, missed flight)
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Oh no, that's awful! I'm really sorry — what did the airline say in the end?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: How interesting! Well, at least you got to see a new country.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A positive, light reaction to bad news reads as mocking or out of touch; the register and polarity of the reaction (sympathetic pitch drop for 'Oh no, that's awful') must match the valence of the news.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: A colleague announces they got a promotion
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: That's fantastic! I'm so pleased for you — when do you start in the new role?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: Mm. Okay. That's fine then. (flat, level tone)
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: A monotone flat delivery of neutral fillers reads as sarcasm or resentment towards good news; a wide pitch range + bright, higher energy conveys genuine enthusiasm.

communication_tips: Find common ground (shared context, weather, event, or surroundings).
Match the other speaker's mood and energy level.
Give extra information beyond one-word answers ('Yes'/'No') to keep the conversation moving.
Pay attention and ask questions back.

pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_textbook: Tell me the cause of this phenomenon.
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: Why do you think that's happening? / What's the main reason behind it?
pragmatic_contrasts.pedagogical_reason: In everyday discussion, 'Why do you think...' or 'How come...' sounds much more natural than formal nominalizations.

pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_textbook: Your explanation is wrong because of an exception.
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: be true for [group A], but what about [group B]?
pragmatic_contrasts.pedagogical_reason: Conceding partial truth before raising an exception keeps collaborative inquiry natural and constructive.

communication_tips: Use light probing questions in Turn 2 ('Why do you think...?', 'What's behind...?') so the causal discussion starts naturally.
In Turn 4, acknowledge the first factor before introducing an exception ('That's true for A, but what about B?').
Keep Turn 5 focused on a clear condition ('depend on...', 'mostly happen when...') rather than repeating Turn 3.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Opening a friendly campus or part-time interview
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: What made you apply for...? / What got you interested in joining...?
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: State your purpose for applying.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Friendly interviews open with natural conversational questions rather than stiff bureaucratic commands.

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Discussing limited experience or a busy day
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: I haven't done X directly, but I pick things up quickly / I'm a bit tight on Mondays, but Fridays are light.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I have no experience. / I cannot come.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: In interviews, pair any limitation or schedule constraint with a positive alternative or willingness to learn.

communication_tips: In a natural interview, the interviewer briefly reacts to the applicant's answer ('That's great—', 'Good to know—') before asking the next question.
Applicants can either highlight direct experience OR honestly state they are new to a task while showing enthusiasm and transferable skills.

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 1 (Turns 1-2: Opening & Purpose)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: Why Speaker 2 is interested in applying for the role or club (Turns 1-2)

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (paraphrase the opening purpose, motivation, or situation actually established in Turns 1-2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (use a detail mentioned later in the dialogue as if it were the opening reason)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Speaker / Role Swap (swap the roles, intentions, or situations of Speaker 1 and Speaker 2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Tone / Polarity Flip (misread the speaker's opening attitude or flip affirmative/negative intent)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 2 (Turns 3-4: Key Question, Point or Constraint)
question_blueprint_template.comprehension_focus: What background experience or skill Speaker 1 asks about

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (accurately restate the specific question, requirement, or point Speaker 1 raises around Turn 3)
option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Opposite Detail / Polarity Flip (invert the key detail, timeframe, or condition mentioned in the dialogue)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (borrow a detail from Turns 5-8 that belongs to a different point)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Overstatement / Scope Distortion (exaggerate a reasonable question or requirement into an extreme rule)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 2 (Turns 3-4: Speaker 2's Response, Experience or Stance)

option_slot_operators.distractor_1_operator: Opposite Stance / Experience Flip (claim the opposite of what Speaker 2 actually said about their experience or view)
option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Speaker / Role Swap (attribute Speaker 1's words or expectations to Speaker 2)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Cross-Turn Detail Mix-up (mix in a detail from another turn out of context)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 3 (Turns 5-6: Practical Arrangement, Condition or Follow-Up)

option_slot_operators.correct_operator: Paraphrase Operator (capture the schedule, method, or conditional arrangement actually discussed across Turns 5-6)

option_slot_operators.distractor_2_operator: Unadopted / Confused Detail Trap (present a busy conflict or rejected option as the agreed plan)
option_slot_operators.distractor_3_operator: Overstatement Trap (turn a specific or conditional statement into an extreme absolute)

question_blueprint_template.anchor_phase: Phase 4 (Turns 7-8: Next Steps & Closing Outcome)

pragmatic_contrasts.situation: Answering a reflection or weakness question in a professional interview
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: That's a fair question—in hindsight, I'd have built in a buffer / involved the team earlier.
pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_blunt: I have no weaknesses and everything went perfectly.
pragmatic_contrasts.pragmatic_note: Demonstrating candid self-reflection ('in hindsight, I'd have...') sounds far more authentic and credible than claiming perfection.

communication_tips: Keep the interview cohesive around one concrete role/project thread from Turn 1 to Turn 8 so each follow-up question builds naturally on the candidate's previous answer.
Candidates can share either a strong success or a candid trade-off/lesson learned ('in hindsight...', 'we were tight on..., so we pivoted to...').

pragmatic_contrasts.avoid_stiff_or_textbook: Your price is too expensive. Make it cheaper.
pragmatic_contrasts.prefer_authentic_spoken: That's a bit over my budget—is there any room to go a little lower if I...?
pragmatic_contrasts.pedagogical_reason: Polite bargaining frames the constraint around one's own budget and offers a practical condition rather than criticizing the other person.

communication_tips: Frame budget limits around your own constraints ('a bit over my budget') rather than criticizing the offer.
Pair every request for a lower price with a practical trade-off ('if I pick it up / book early').
Confirm the exact agreed terms before closing the conversation.
